d.title: The same total, collapsed and kept
d.caption: GROUP BY and a window function compute the identical number. GROUP BY spends the rows to get it; the window writes it onto every row that is already there — which is what lets the next column compare a row with its own group's total.

d.title: Where a window function is allowed
d.caption: A window function is computed at the SELECT step, after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING have all finished. Everything in this table follows from that one fact — including why filtering on a rank needs an outer query.

d.title: Quentin and Rosa both earn 125,000
d.caption: The three functions agree everywhere except at the tie, and the row *after* the tie is where they separate: ROW_NUMBER has spent two numbers, RANK skips the one the tie consumed, DENSE_RANK skips nothing. Ask for 'the top three' and you get three, four or four rows.

d.title: Which ranking function the question wants
d.caption: The choice is decided by what a tie should mean. 'Second-highest salary' is the second distinct *value*, so a tie at the top still leaves a second value below it — DENSE_RANK. 'Exactly three rows' can only be ROW_NUMBER.

d.title: The default frame is RANGE, and it swallows the tie
d.caption: Writing `ORDER BY salary` with no frame gives `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`, and under RANGE the rows that tie with the current row are peers — so Quentin's running total already includes Rosa. Spell `ROWS` and his total stops at him. Both numbers are real; only one is the one you meant.

d.title: Four ways to bound a frame
d.caption: ROWS counts rows and is blind to ties. RANGE measures the sort key itself, so tied rows always share a frame. GROUPS counts peer groups. The distinction only shows up when the sort key has duplicates — which real data always does.
cells: a moving average of n rows

d.title: Reading a value from another row
d.caption: Each of these reads one value from one row of the window rather than aggregating over it. The third argument of LAG and LEAD is the default used at the edge, which is how you avoid a NULL on the first row of every partition.

d.title: Why LAST_VALUE returns the current row
d.caption: FIRST_VALUE looks backwards into a frame that starts at the partition's beginning, so it works. LAST_VALUE looks forwards into a frame that **ends at the current row** — so the last row of the frame is the current row, and the function returns the value you already had.

d.title: Sessionisation: a flag becomes a running sum becomes an id
d.caption: One idea, applied three times: the output of a window function is an ordinary column, so the next window function can run over it. No self-joins and no trip to Python.

d.title: Gaps and islands: why subtracting a row number finds a streak
d.caption: Consecutive days advance by one, and so does the row number — so their difference is constant for the length of a run and changes the moment a day is missed. The constant is meaningless on its own and is a perfect group key.

items.label: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day)
items.desc: 1, 2, 3, 4 ... in date order

items.label: day - rn (as an interval)
items.desc: constant while the days are consecutive

items.label: A missed day advances day but not rn
items.desc: so the difference jumps to a new constant

items.label: GROUP BY that difference
items.desc: one group per unbroken run

items.label: COUNT(*) and MIN(day) per group
items.desc: the length of each streak and when it began

d.title: A pipeline read top to bottom instead of inside out
d.caption: Three nested derived tables and three chained CTEs produce the same plan. The difference is that each step has a name, and the grain of each step can be written next to it — which is where the fan-out bugs of 2.2 get caught before they ship.

items.desc: grain: unchanged, one column added

d.caption: They sit on one spectrum: how long the name lasts. A CTE and a derived table are the same thing with different ergonomics; a view is a CTE that outlives the statement; a temp table is a view that has been computed once and can be indexed.

d.title: A recursive CTE, round by round
d.caption: The recursive member never sees the whole result — only the rows the previous round produced. That is what makes termination possible, and what makes a cycle fatal: the working set never empties.

items.label: The anchor runs once
items.desc: its rows become the first working set

items.label: The recursive member runs on the working set
items.desc: it joins those rows to the table again

items.label: Its output becomes the new working set
items.desc: the previous one is kept in the result

items.label: Repeat
items.desc: each round reaches one level deeper

items.label: A round produces no rows
items.desc: the recursion stops and the union is the answer

items.label: A cycle means it never produces none
items.desc: it runs until the engine's depth limit or forever

d.title: Three ways to survive a cycle
d.caption: A tree terminates because leaves have no children. A graph does not: with the edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, the working set is never empty. Each of these breaks the loop by carrying the path so far, so a node that reappears can be detected.
cells: the depth limit, or the query is killed
